reference.source: Firestein & Kelley's Textbook of Rheumatology / EULAR recommendations for autoinflammatory diseases
clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant autoinflammatory disorder caused by mutations in TNFRSF1A, encoding the type 1 tumour necrosis factor receptor
Fever episodes are characteristically prolonged, often lasting one to three weeks, distinguishing it from the shorter attacks of other periodic fever syndromes
A migratory, tender erythematous rash overlying underlying myalgia, typically moving distally along a limb, is a suggestive feature
Periorbital oedema with conjunctivitis or periorbital pain is a classic ocular manifestation
Attacks commonly include serositis (abdominal and chest pain), arthralgia and monocytic fasciitis
AA (secondary) amyloidosis is the major long-term complication, driven by chronic inflammation, and warrants surveillance
Therapy is directed at the interleukin-1 axis and, in some cases, interleukin-6 blockade, whereas continuous tumour necrosis factor inhibition has been less reliably effective
reference.pathophysiology: TRAPS is an autosomal dominant autoinflammatory syndrome caused by mutations in TNFRSF1A, the gene for the 55-kDa tumour necrosis factor receptor 1. Rather than a simple loss of receptor shedding, the mutant receptor misfolds and is retained within the endoplasmic reticulum, provoking a cellular stress response, enhanced production of reactive oxygen species, and ligand-independent, exaggerated pro-inflammatory signalling. This drives excess innate cytokine output, particularly along the interleukin-1 pathway, producing recurrent systemic inflammation. Persistent elevation of acute phase proteins over years predisposes to deposition of serum amyloid A protein in tissues and the development of AA amyloidosis.
additionalDifferentials: Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis or adult-onset Still disease
Cyclical or infective causes of recurrent fever
Inflammatory bowel disease presenting with recurrent abdominal pain and fever
additionalInvestigations: Acute phase reactants (C-reactive protein and serum amyloid A) during and between attacks
Full blood count showing neutrophilia during attacks
Urinalysis for proteinuria as an early marker of AA amyloidosis
Serum immunoglobulins including IgD to help distinguish related syndromes
Tissue biopsy with amyloid staining where amyloidosis is suspected
redFlags: New or increasing proteinuria suggesting evolving AA amyloidosis
Persistently elevated inflammatory markers between attacks indicating uncontrolled subclinical inflammation
Severe serositis mimicking an acute surgical abdomen
reference.prognosis: With effective anti-inflammatory therapy attacks can be controlled and quality of life preserved, but untreated or poorly controlled disease carries a meaningful risk of AA amyloidosis and consequent renal failure, which is the principal determinant of long-term outcome.
pitfalls: Expecting brief attacks and dismissing TRAPS because fevers are unusually prolonged
Failing to monitor for proteinuria and missing early amyloidosis
Assuming tumour necrosis factor blockade is always effective, when interleukin-1 targeting is often preferred
Repeated surgery for recurrent serositis mistaken for a surgical abdomen
references: EULAR recommendations for the management of autoinflammatory diseases
management: Interleukin-1 inhibition with anakinra or canakinumab as the mainstay to suppress attacks and normalise acute-phase proteins
Corticosteroids to shorten acute attacks and NSAIDs for symptomatic control of fever and serositis
Consider etanercept where IL-1 blockade is not accessible, avoiding monoclonal anti-TNF agents such as infliximab
Surveillance for AA amyloidosis with serum amyloid A between attacks and urinary protein screening for early nephropathy
Genetic counselling and TNFRSF1A testing of at-risk family members given autosomal dominant transmission
Rheumatology or clinical immunology coordination with nephrology referral if renal amyloid develops
Escalate to continuous biologic therapy for persistent subclinical inflammation to protect against amyloid deposition
